top_choice_rationale: P002 (Calvo, Taylor, Woodford) credits three separable building blocks of the nominal-rigidity framework: time-dependent pricing, staggered contracts with an interest-rate rule, and the welfare-based policy synthesis. Each has an identifiable originating body of work and 25 to 40 years of extension, criticism and use in policy analysis. With the citation confined to rigidity theory and policy rules, and no claim about the Phillips-curve slope or forecasting, the post-2008 and 2021-23 inflation debates affect parameterisation rather than the contribution. The main cost is real: Galí, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets are omitted under the three-name cap. I judge that choosing the originators over the estimation strand is defensible on originality, separability and durability. P001 (Helpman, Melitz) is second because of its clean two-person credit line and mature mechanism. Its weaknesses are the uncredited Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum lineage and welfare magnitudes that depend on functional form. P003 follows because its trade-shock evidence is well identified, but the task-framework credit sits partly outside the ballot and aggregate magnitudes are still debated. P004 is fourth because of partly observational cross-country identification and partial overlap with the 2024 prize. No award is last because every proposal on the slate is a mature, substantive achievement.
recusal_note: Profile-based connections, disclosed and not adjudicated: I am a frequent co-author of John Hassler (chair) and Timo Boppart (co-opted member) and an IIES colleague of both. Boppart and I both rank P002 first, and Hassler's first choice is P004. None of the credited laureates on any proposal (Calvo, Taylor, Woodford, Helpman, Melitz, Autor, Dorn, Hanson, Persson, Tabellini, Besley) is a documented co-author of mine. My macro field is close to P002, which I treat as possible bias, and I applied the common criteria across fields.
